blocks.text: An action potential is initiated at the axonal hillock when synaptic signals received by the dendrites and soma are enough to raise the intracellular resting membrane potential from -70 mV to the threshold potential of -55 mV.
At -55 mV the Na+ channels at the axon initial segment open; the Na+ influx rapidly reverses the membrane potential from negative values to +40 mV.
At +40 mV the Na+ channels close and voltage-gated K+ channels open; K+ moving out of the axon repolarises the cell membrane.

blocks.title: Action potential sequence (as given in the notes)
rows: Threshold: Na+ channels at the initial segment open; Na+ influx
Na+ channels close; voltage-gated K+ channels open; K+ efflux repolarises the membrane

blocks.text: Repolarisation is the potassium route: the correct statement is that the membrane repolarises with K+ moving **OUT** of the cell. Rapid sodium entry is what drives the upstroke (threshold about -55 mV opens voltage-gated Na+ channels, bringing the potential to a positive value), and restoration comes from delayed opening of voltage-gated K+ channels plus closing of Na+ channels - the options that pair repolarisation with Na+ entry, depolarisation with K+ entry, or Na+ moving out are all wrong.

blocks.note: Notes do not state which ion is highest inside the cell. **Q20**: potassium is greatest inside the cell (more K+ inside, more Na+ outside; the Na-K pump moves Na out and K in).
Notes give no ion permeabilities. **Q38** explanation: K+ relatively permeable, Na+ relatively impermeable, Cl- freely permeable, organic ions relatively impermeable.

items.text: Resting membrane potential is -70 mV (intracellular side relative to extracellular) - not +70 or +170 mV.
At rest potassium is the ion greatest in concentration inside the cell (sodium is greater outside; the Na-K pump moves Na out, K in).
Chloride is the ion freely permeable across the membrane (K+ relatively permeable, Na+ and organic ions relatively impermeable).

bullets.text: Resting potential -70 mV; threshold -55 mV; initiated at the axonal hillock.
Threshold: Na+ channels at the initial segment open; influx drives potential to +40 mV.
At +40 mV Na+ channels close and voltage-gated K+ channels open; K+ efflux repolarises.
Exam: repolarisation = K+ moving out (Q30); resting potential about -70 mV (Q6).

blocks.text: A synapse is a junction between 2 nerve cells. Three types of synapses are noted in the nervous system: chemical, electrical and conjoint.

blocks.title: Types of synapse
rows: Presynaptic neuron releases a chemical molecule on stimulation; it acts on the next neuron to bring on a molecular effect or propagate the impulse downstream
Bring on the response by electrical communication without chemical exchange
Have both electrical and chemical properties

blocks.text: Chemical synapses are excitatory or inhibitory according to their effect on the postsynaptic neuron: excitatory synaptic activity depolarises postsynaptic neurons; inhibitory activity hyperpolarises them.

Postsynaptic changes from an excitatory synapse may not be enough to induce an action potential but can facilitate the likelihood of one with further stimulation (facilitation). Input from several other presynaptic cells can give spatial summation leading to an action potential; recurrent stimulation by the same synapse can give temporal summation.

bullets.text: 3 synapse types: chemical, electrical (no chemical exchange), conjoint (both).
Excitatory synapse = depolarises; inhibitory = hyperpolarises.
Facilitation: sub-threshold excitatory change makes a later action potential more likely.
Spatial summation = input from several presynaptic cells; temporal summation = repeated stimulation by the same synapse.

blocks.text: Cholecystokinin is the gut hormone that answers a stem about a hormone released from the small intestine in response to fats and proteins to regulate food intake: the explanation says **CCK** inhibits food intake by stimulating the vagal nerve and inhibiting gastric emptying, and central **CCK** receptors can also inhibit eating - consistent with **CCK** sitting in the anorexigenic (satiety) column of the notes, not the orexigenic one.

blocks.note: Notes list leptin only as an anorexigenic mediator. Mock **Q65** (binge eating, body image disturbance, weight-reducing measures = bulimia nervosa): reduced leptin is the answer - the explanation says patients with bulimia nervosa and those recovered from it had significantly lower serum leptin than **BMI**-matched controls, consistent with decreased leptin function contributing to impaired postingestion satiety, neuroendocrine abnormalities and low resting metabolic rate.

blocks.text: Ghrelin is the only orexigenic substance produced outside the **CNS** - it is synthesised in the gastric mucosa; adipose cells synthesise leptin.

Food and food cues increase dopaminergic activity in the nucleus accumbens (reward centre). Destruction of dopamine pathways reduces eating behaviour. In obesity, **D2** receptors are reduced in the striatum.

bullets.text: Ventromedial hypothalamus = satiety centre; lateral hypothalamus = feeding centre.
Orexigenic: ghrelin, neuropeptide Y. Anorexigenic: leptin, CCK, serotonin.
Ghrelin: only orexigenic substance made outside CNS (gastric mucosa); leptin from adipose cells.
Food cues raise nucleus accumbens dopamine; obesity has reduced striatal D2 receptors.

blocks.title: Hypothalamic temperature centres
rows: Parasympathetic-mediated sweating and vasodilation, resulting in hypothermia
Sympathetic drive, shivering and vasoconstriction, leading to hyperthermia

blocks.text: Body temperature varies diurnally; lesions in the median eminence reduce the diurnal temperature variation.
Certain drugs can induce malignant hyperthermia, but not through a hypothalamic mechanism - an abnormal excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscles is responsible.
Hyperthermia is also seen in Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (**NMS**), induced by neuroleptic use or **levodopa** withdrawal.

bullets.text: Preoptic anterior hypothalamus = hypothermic centre (sweating, vasodilation).
Posterior hypothalamus = hyperthermic centre (shivering, vasoconstriction, sympathetic drive).
Median eminence lesions reduce diurnal temperature variation.
Malignant hyperthermia: skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling defect, not hypothalamic.
NMS hyperthermia: neuroleptics or levodopa withdrawal.

blocks.text: Thalamus plays a crucial role in pain perception; higher cortical centres are central to localisation and interpretation of the pain signal.

blocks.title: Pain pathways
rows: Thin unmyelinated C fibres or sparsely myelinated A-delta fibres carry pain to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord

blocks.text: Opioid receptors in the dorsal horn and possibly the brain stem (periaqueductal grey matter) modulate pain intensity. Descending fibres from serotonergic raphe nuclei also modulate pain perception; this may explain the role of tricyclic drugs in reducing chronic pain.

Thalamic pain syndrome can occur in stroke involving thalamoperforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery: contralateral loss of sensation with burning or aching pain triggered by light cutaneous stimulation.

bullets.text: Thalamus: pain perception; cortex: localisation and interpretation.
C fibres and A-delta fibres carry pain to the dorsal horn.
Fast = lateral spinothalamic (localisation); slow = reticulothalamic (subjective sensation).
Dorsal horn and periaqueductal grey opioid receptors modulate pain; serotonergic raphe descending fibres may explain tricyclic effect in chronic pain.
Thalamic pain syndrome: PCA thalamoperforating stroke; contralateral sensory loss with burning pain on light touch.

sections.title: 6. Neural basis of thirst and ADH

blocks.text: The subfornical organ (**SFO**) and organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis (**OVLT**) are circumventricular organs playing a crucial role in the perception of thirst; the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus is also involved.
Angiotensin **II** acts as a neurotransmitter to propagate thirst signals to the hypothalamus. Hypotension also stimulates thirst through pathways from baroreceptors on the aorta and carotid.
**ADH** increases water reabsorption at renal tubules and so helps maintain fluid balance.

blocks.title: SIADH
rows: Damage to paraventricular and supraoptic hypothalamic nuclei; drugs such as **carbamazepine** or **chlorpromazine**; tumours such as carcinoma of lung
Low sodium and reduced osmolarity with normal renal sodium excretion and high urine osmolality

bullets.text: Thirst: SFO and OVLT (circumventricular organs) plus paraventricular nucleus.
Angiotensin II propagates thirst signals; hypotension stimulates thirst via aortic/carotid baroreceptors.
ADH raises renal water reabsorption.
SIADH: hypothalamic nuclei damage, carbamazepine, chlorpromazine, lung carcinoma; low Na and osmolarity with high urine osmolality.

blocks.caption: Table (page 4, "E. Abnormalities in physiological drives"): columns Disorder / Clinical features; rows Kluver-Bucy syndrome, Laurence-Moon-Biedl Syndrome, Prader-Willi Syndrome, Kleine-Levin Syndrome, Psychogenic polydipsia.

blocks.title: Disorders of physiological drives
rows: Bilateral lesions of amygdala and hippocampus: placidity with decreased aggressive behaviour; prominent oral exploratory behaviour and hypersexuality; hypermetamorphosis (objects repeatedly examined as if novel)
Obesity and hypogonadism with low **IQ**, retinitis pigmentosa and polydactyly; diabetes insipidus also seen; autosomal recessive, locus 11q13 in most cases; no hypothalamic lesions found

Hypotonia, obesity with hyperphagia, hypogenitalism, mental retardation, short stature, impaired glucose tolerance; abnormal temperature control and daytime hypersomnolence related to hypothalamic disturbance; reduced oxytocin neurons and satiety neurons; paternal deletion (genomic imprinting) at 15q11-q13

Compulsive eating with hyperphagia, hypersomnolence, hyperactivity, hypersexuality and exhibitionism; a hypothalamic abnormality sometimes preceded by a viral illness; often resolves by the third decade of life
Excessive water consumption in the absence of hypovolemia or hypernatremia; may lead to water intoxication and serious electrolyte imbalance

blocks.text: Hypertension is the **INCORRECT** Kleine-Levin feature to spot: episodic nature, hypersomnia, male predominance and hyperphagia are all features (a rare syndrome of periodic somnolence and morbid hunger, almost exclusively in male adolescents, attacks lasting days to weeks).

blocks.subtopic: Kleine-Levin: male predominance and episodic course
blocks.note: Notes do not mention episodic nature or male predominance. **Q50** explanation: a rare syndrome of periodic somnolence and morbid hunger, almost exclusively in male adolescents, with attacks lasting days to weeks.

bullets.text: Kluver-Bucy: bilateral amygdala/hippocampus lesions; placidity, oral exploration, hypersexuality, hypermetamorphosis.
Laurence-Moon-Biedl: obesity, hypogonadism, low IQ, retinitis pigmentosa, polydactyly; AR, 11q13.
Prader-Willi: hypotonia, hyperphagia/obesity; paternal deletion 15q11-q13; reduced oxytocin and satiety neurons.
Kleine-Levin: hyperphagia, hypersomnolence, hypersexuality; often resolves by third decade.
Psychogenic polydipsia: excess water without hypovolemia/hypernatremia; water intoxication risk.

blocks.text: Early fetal life is a prolific period of neurogenesis; an active zone of nerve cell production (the subventricular zone) lies immediately around the ventricles of the neural tube. Neurons produced here migrate outwards to the cortical plate.

Thalamic axons projecting to the cortical plate first synapse on transient subplate neurons; normally they then detach, proceed superficially to the true cortical cells, and the subplate neurons degenerate. In some patients with schizophrenia abnormal persistence of subplate neurons has been noted, suggesting failure of axonal path-finding.

Continuous neurogenesis occurs in adults in certain regions (particularly the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus and the olfactory bulb). Stress reduces hippocampal neurogenesis; enriched environments, exercise and antidepressants promote it. Whether adult neurogenesis occurs in other regions is controversial.

Neuronal migration takes place in the first 6 months of gestation. Radial migration is the primary mechanism by which excitatory neurons reach the cortex; radial glial cells form scaffolding through their foot processes. Successive populations travel past earlier ones (inside-out pattern) to form radial stacks (Rakic cortical columns).
Most inhibitory interneurons in the external and internal granular layers are tangentially migrated neurons. Abnormal migration leaves neurons in ectopic positions (heterotopia).

Myelination begins prenatally at about the 4th gestational month; it is largely complete in early childhood (by 2 years) but does not reach full extent, especially in association cortices, until late in the third decade of life.

bullets.text: Neurogenesis starts in the subventricular zone; neurons migrate to the cortical plate.
Persistent subplate neurons seen in some schizophrenia - failure of axonal path-finding.
Adult neurogenesis: dentate gyrus and olfactory bulb; stress reduces, exercise/enrichment/antidepressants promote.
Migration in first 6 months of gestation; radial (excitatory, inside-out) vs tangential (most inhibitory interneurons).
Failed migration = heterotopia.
Myelination from about 4th gestational month; largely complete by 2 years; association cortex into third decade.

blocks.text: Synaptogenesis occurs very rapidly from the second trimester through the first ten years of life, peaking within the first 2 postnatal years. By mid-childhood more neurons and cellular processes exist than the adult brain requires; synaptic pruning then selects and preserves the most useful connections and continues through the early teen years.
Before 5 years of age **D2** receptor density is greater than adult levels, regressing during the second decade.

Dopamine receptors continue to decrease in adult years at a slower rate (==2.2%== reduction per decade), faster in males than females. In schizophrenia the rate of **D2** receptor loss is faster (==6.0%== per decade) than in healthy men.

blocks.title: Pruning abnormalities
rows: Relative under-pruning; size of certain brain regions may be larger than in healthy controls

blocks.text: Cerebral plasticity is the capability of the brain to be moulded. Cortical sensory maps change with variations in sensory input; in phantom limb, the amputated limb representation may occur on the cortical face area. Repeated practice reorganises functional regions (e.g. musicians, jugglers).

bullets.text: Synaptogenesis peaks in first 2 postnatal years; pruning from mid-childhood through early teens.
D2 density above adult levels before age 5, regressing in the second decade.
Adult D2 loss 2.2% per decade (faster in males); schizophrenia 6.0% per decade.
Excessive pruning = schizophrenia; under-pruning = autism.
Plasticity: sensory maps change with input; phantom limb maps onto cortical face area; practice reorganises regions.

blocks.text: The anterior pituitary lobe secretes hormones regulated by neurohormones from parvocellular hypothalamic neurons. The posterior lobe releases 2 hormones synthesised in magnocellular cells of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei.

blocks.caption: Table (page 7): Region / Hormonal output. Anterior pituitary: GH, LH, FSH, ACTH, TSH, Prolactin. Posterior pituitary: Vasopressin (ADH), Oxytocin. Hypothalamus: CRH, GHRH, GnRH, TRH, SST (inhibits GH), PIF (prolactin inhibitory factor, dopamine).

blocks.text: Growth hormone excess causes acromegaly in adults or gigantism in children; low levels are associated with dwarfism. Exercise, sleep and stress increase **GH** release. **GH** response to **GHRH** and sleep-associated **GH** release are altered in depression and anorexia nervosa.

Prolactin release is inhibited by hypothalamic dopamine; **TRH** may facilitate it. Levels rise in pregnancy, nursing, sleep and exercise. Antipsychotics block **D2** receptors in the tuberoinfundibular tract, removing dopamine inhibition: hyperprolactinaemia, gynaecomastia in males, galactorrhoea in females; long-standing increase may lead to osteoporosis.

Vasopressin (**ADH**) and oxytocin are peptides differing in only two amino acids. Vasopressin is thought to play a role in attention, memory and learning; its release is increased by pain, stress, exercise, morphine, nicotine and barbiturates and decreased by alcohol. Oxytocin is implicated in mammalian bonding, maternal behaviour, social bonding and sexual receptivity.

Oxytocin is the posterior pituitary hormone in a list that also offers **melatonin**, gonadotrophin, prolactin and testosterone - gonadotrophins and prolactin sit in the anterior pituitary row of the notes. Oxytocin and vasopressin neurons are in the magnocellular paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei and project to the neurohypophysis.

Vasopressin is the answer when a stem asks for a substance that is both a **CNS** neurotransmitter and a hormone: the explanation notes that oxytocin/vasopressin are made in magnocellular **PVN** and supraoptic neurons and released into the bloodstream, where they act like hormones on peripheral targets (glucagon, serotonin, dopamine and thyroxine are the other options).

blocks.note: Notes do not cover the work-up of secondary amenorrhoea. **Q26**: the most common cause is pregnancy (pregnancy test is the investigation of choice); anticonvulsants used in bipolar disorder can reduce oral contraceptive efficacy.

bullets.text: Posterior pituitary: vasopressin and oxytocin (made in supraoptic/paraventricular magnocellular cells).
Anterior pituitary: GH, LH, FSH, ACTH, TSH, prolactin.
Prolactin inhibited by dopamine; antipsychotic D2 blockade in tuberoinfundibular tract causes hyperprolactinaemia.
GH excess: acromegaly (adults) / gigantism (children).
Vasopressin and oxytocin differ by two amino acids; vasopressin released by pain, stress, nicotine, barbiturates, reduced by alcohol.

blocks.text: **TRH** from the hypothalamus stimulates **TSH** secretion from the pituitary; **TSH** stimulates the thyroid to synthesise and release **T4** and **T3**. **T4** is the predominant form but **T3** is biologically more potent; **T4** is converted into **T3** by target organs and the brain.
Exogenous **TRH** normally produces a brisk **TSH** rise. A blunted **TRH** response is seen in depression, and also in mania, alcohol withdrawal and anorexia.

**T3** and **T4** supplements added to antidepressant treatment have accelerated response in some patients, particularly women; exogenous thyroid hormone (e.g. in resistant depression) increases serotonergic transmission with decreased 5-**HT1A** and increased 5-**HT2A** sensitivity. Nerve growth factor genes are activated by **T3** in early development but not in the adult brain.

**Lithium** produces hypothyroidism, especially in middle-aged women predisposed by antithyroid autoantibodies. Hypothyroidism is sometimes implicated in rapid cycling in previously stable bipolar patients; hyperthyroidism is associated with generalised anxiety symptoms.

blocks.caption: Two-column table (page 8): Hyperthyroidism vs Hypothyroidism, each with a Physical symptoms row and a Mental symptoms row.

blocks.title: Hyperthyroidism vs hypothyroidism
rows: Tachycardia, weight loss, heat intolerance, sweating
Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin
Anxiety, irritability, poor concentration, agitation, emotional lability
Depression, reduced activity (psychomotor retardation), reduced libido, poor memory

blocks.text: Tachycardia is the option inconsistent with hypothyroidism: increased **TSH**, cold intolerance, decreased libido and weight gain all fit. The explanation lists bradycardia as a possible sign (and primary hypothyroidism as **TSH** above the reference range); the notes place tachycardia under hyperthyroidism.

blocks.note: Notes do not list bradycardia or raised **TSH**. **Q46** explanation: signs may include bradycardia; primary hypothyroidism is defined by **TSH** above the reference range; common symptoms also include lethargy, constipation, voice change.

bullets.text: HPT axis: TRH -> TSH -> T4/T3; T4 predominant, T3 more potent.
Blunted TRH response: depression, mania, alcohol withdrawal, anorexia.
T3/T4 augmentation of antidepressants can speed response (esp. women).
Lithium causes hypothyroidism (middle-aged women, antithyroid antibodies); hypothyroidism linked to rapid cycling.
Hyperthyroid: tachycardia, weight loss, anxiety; hypothyroid: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, depression.

sections.title: 12. Neuroendocrinology: adrenal cortex and the HPA axis

blocks.text: **CRH** from the hypothalamus stimulates **ACTH** release from the anterior pituitary; **ACTH** stimulates cortisol release from the adrenal cortex; cortisol inhibits both **CRH** and **ACTH** by negative feedback (the **HPA** axis).

The **HPA** axis regulates the stress response. In chronic stress feedback fails and excess cortisol harms the hippocampus (glucocorticoid receptors abundant): decreased neurogenesis and dendritic atrophy shrink the hippocampus, disrupting long-term potentiation and impairing memory. A compensatory rise in dendritic arborisation in the basolateral amygdala may contribute to memory bias towards negative events.
Cortisol shows diurnal variation with peak levels around 6:00-7:00 **AM**.

Hypercortisolaemia with loss of diurnal variation is reported in depression (especially melancholic with somatic syndrome), some patients with mania (especially psychotic), **OCD** and schizoaffective disorder. Hypocortisolaemia is seen in a subgroup of **PTSD** (possibly aberrant pituitary feedback from excessive glucocorticoid receptors - probably a genetic vulnerability); low cortisol is also seen in chronic fatigue and fibromyalgia.

blocks.caption: Two-column table (page 9): Hypercortisolism (Addison's disease) vs Hypocortisolism (Cushing's syndrome), each with Physical symptoms and Mental symptoms rows, as printed.

blocks.title: Cortisol state tables as printed in the notes
rows: Anxiety, irritability, poor concentration, agitation, emotional lability
Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin
Depression, mania, confusion, and psychotic symptoms

blocks.note: The source table pairs hypercortisolism with Addison disease and hypocortisolism with Cushing syndrome, but the same notes (p9, **DST** section) call Cushing syndrome an organic hypercortisolaemic state, and **Q48** explanation describes Addison disease as glucocorticoid and/or mineralocorticoid deficiency. Treat the printed labels as a likely error and verify before relying on it.

Notes give no electrolytes. **Q48**: apathy, weight loss, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia suggest Addison disease; explanation adds dehydration, hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and psychiatric symptoms apathy, anhedonia, fatigue, depressed mood.

blocks.text: **PTSD** is the answer for **LOW** cortisol, the opposite of the usual chronic-stress rise: although increased cortisol is typically linked with chronic stress, **PTSD** is often linked with lower cortisol, and lower cortisol shortly after trauma predicts subsequent **PTSD** severity. Depression, mania and psychosis are among the distractor options.

Raised **ACTH** and **CRF** together point to depression: the explanation calls elevated **HPA** activity one of the clearest links between depression and the biology of chronic stress (chronic hyperactivity leads to excessive glucocorticoid release).

The correct statement on depression is that about ==50%== of patients show raised cortisol (hypercortisolaemia); the other four options (large cortisol dose exacerbating symptoms, low **CRF** in "**CS**", low **DHEA**, adrenal cortex atrophy in ==20%==) are wrong.
Peak cortisol is about 6 **AM** (6:00-7:00 **AM**) - not 9 **AM** after breakfast, midday, 6 **PM** or midnight - and the same fact is asked again in a second question.

Apathy and weight loss with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia = Addison disease, not Cushing syndrome: Addison disease is chronic glucocorticoid and/or mineralocorticoid deficiency (hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, dehydration, hypotension, hyperpigmentation; psychiatric features apathy, anhedonia, fatigue, depressed mood). Do not follow the notes' printed table that pairs Addison with hypercortisolism (see the gap above).

Postural hypotension, anorexia, nausea and weakness with apathy, anhedonia, fatigue and depressed mood = Addison syndrome (corticosteroid deficiency), which can be mistaken for depressive disorder: vomiting is almost never due to isolated depression.

Purplish abdominal striae, nuchal fat and hypomania in a long-standing asthmatic on oral prednisolone = Cushing syndrome, most likely due to the oral prednisolone, **NOT** the inhaled budesonide; theophylline-induced epileptiform activity, late-onset bipolar disorder, hypothyroidism and secondary diabetes are distractors.

blocks.note: Notes give no test. Mock **Q65** (gradual skin darkening over scars, skin folds and pressure points, extreme fatigue, weakness and weight loss after a trivial accident): the **ACTH** stimulation test is the most commonly used definitive test for adrenal insufficiency. Blood and/or urine cortisol is measured before and after synthetic **ACTH**; normally cortisol rises, whereas people with Addison disease or long-standing secondary adrenal insufficiency show little or no rise.

Notes do not cover adrenal enzyme defects. Mock **Q40**: female pseudo-hermaphroditism (female gonadal sex with masculinised external genitalia due to high androgen levels) is most commonly caused by the virilising congenital adrenal hyperplasias (genetic defects of steroidogenesis).

bullets.text: HPA axis: CRH -> ACTH -> cortisol, with cortisol negative feedback on CRH and ACTH.
Chronic stress: feedback fails; hippocampal atrophy, impaired LTP and memory; amygdala dendritic growth biases to negative events.
Cortisol peaks around 6-7 AM.
Hypercortisolaemia: depression (melancholic), psychotic mania, OCD, schizoaffective.
Hypocortisolaemia: subgroup of PTSD, chronic fatigue, fibromyalgia.
PTSD is the low-cortisol answer; Addison disease (hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, apathy) is cortisol deficiency, not Cushing.

blocks.text: Exogenous corticosteroids such as dexamethasone suppress endogenous cortisol production if the **HPA** axis is intact.

blocks.title: DST protocol as given
rows: 1 mg dexamethasone at 11 **PM**, with baseline cortisol sampling
Any one sample with cortisol >5 mcg/L; shows failed feedback suppression of **ACTH**/**CRH** with continued endogenous cortisol production

blocks.text: **DST** non-suppression is seen in depression and other psychiatric hypercortisolaemic states, and in organic ones such as Cushing syndrome.
Sensitivity for detecting major depression is modest (about 40-==50%==) but higher (about 60-==70%==) in very severe depression with psychotic and melancholic features.

**DST** non-suppression is non-specific: also seen in mania, schizoaffective disorder, major medical conditions, pregnancy, severe weight loss, alcohol, and hepatic enzyme inducers that reduce dexamethasone availability (barbiturates, anticonvulsants and others).
Despite depression, the **DST** may suppress cortisol if the patient has Addison disease or hypopituitarism or takes steroids, high-dose benzodiazepines or indomethacin.

**DST** non-suppression does not increase the likelihood of antidepressant response; a negative test is not a reason to withhold antidepressants. Patients with non-suppression may be less likely to respond to placebo.
Continued failure to suppress cortisol despite apparent recovery from depression suggests increased risk of relapse, poor prognosis and possibly later suicidal behaviour.

After 1 mg dexamethasone at 11 **PM** an intact **HPA** axis shows **SUPPRESSED** **ACTH** (and **CRH**) with falling cortisol; the test detects **FAILURE** of suppression, as in depression and other hypercortisolaemic states including organic ones such as Cushing syndrome. Options that say cortisol increased, **CRH** increased or glucocorticoid receptors blocked describe the abnormal or irrelevant picture.

blocks.note: **Q5** stem says 1 g of dexamethasone while the notes (p9) state 1 mg; the notes figure is the one the explanation matches. Treat the stem as a typo.

bullets.text: DST: 1 mg dexamethasone at 11 PM; cortisol at 8 AM, 4 PM, 11 PM; any >5 mcg/L = non-suppression.
Non-suppression = failed feedback suppression of ACTH/CRH.
Sensitivity for depression about 40-50%; 60-70% in severe psychotic/melancholic depression.
Non-specific: mania, schizoaffective, Cushing, pregnancy, weight loss, alcohol, enzyme inducers.
Does not predict antidepressant response; negative test does not withhold treatment.
Persisting non-suppression after recovery: relapse risk, poor prognosis, later suicidal behaviour.

facts.label: Sensitivity in very severe psychotic/melancholic depression

sections.title: 14. Pineal gland and endocrine changes with sleep

blocks.text: The pineal gland (epiphysis) contains pinealocytes that secrete serotonin (in the day) and **melatonin** (at night); it also contains calcium deposits (corpora arenacea, brain sand) that become more prominent with age.
The pineal gland contains the highest concentration of serotonin in the body. **Melatonin** is synthesised from serotonin by serotonin-N-acetylase and 5-hydroxyindole-O-methyltransferase.

The light-dark cycle is the major regulator of **melatonin** synthesis (increased in darkness). The pineal is regulated by a major beta-adrenergic mechanism, and beta-antagonists such as **propranolol** decrease **melatonin** synthesis.
**Melatonin** regulates circadian rhythms, with both synchronising and phase-shifting properties.

blocks.caption: Shaded box titled "ENDOCRINE CHANGES & SLEEP" (page 10): start of sleep, slow wave sleep, REM sleep, early morning sleep changes, plus the circadian rhythm development note.

expansion: T - Testosterone up at start of sleep
G - **GH** (and **SST**) up in slow wave sleep
P - Prolactin up in early morning sleep

blocks.text: Circadian rhythm development: in the first month the 24-hour core body temperature cycle emerges; by 2 months nocturnal sleeping progresses; by 3 months **melatonin** and cortisol rhythms are established.

**Melatonin** **DECREASES** during **REM** sleep is the correct neuroendocrine-sleep statement; each distractor reverses the notes: testosterone rises (not falls) at sleep onset, **GH** rises (not falls) in slow wave sleep, cortisol is reduced (not up) in slow wave sleep, and prolactin rises (not falls) in early morning sleep.

The nocturnal **GH** surge is in slow wave sleep: the explanation says **GH** is elevated early in a sleep bout, particularly in slow-wave sleep, and decreases in later sleep phases - not **REM**, not stages 1-2, not after waking.

bullets.text: Pineal: serotonin by day, melatonin at night; highest body serotonin; melatonin made from serotonin.
Light-dark cycle regulates melatonin; beta-blockers such as propranolol reduce it.
Sleep: testosterone up at onset; SWS GH and SST up, cortisol down; REM melatonin down; early morning prolactin up.
Circadian development: temperature 1 month; sleep 2 months; melatonin/cortisol rhythms 3 months.

blocks.text: Actigraphy uses a motion sensor to quantify circadian sleep-wake patterns and detect movement disorders during sleep.

Polysomnography (**PSG**) includes **EEG**, **EMG** and **EOG**, and can add **ECG**, oximetry and respiratory monitoring; it helps diagnose and monitor sleep apnoea, narcolepsy, restless legs and **REM** behavioural disorder.

blocks.title: Sleep terms used in PSG
rows: Time from 'lights out' to sleep onset
Time from sleep onset to first **REM** episode; normally about 90 minutes in adults
Time from sleep onset to first non-**REM** episode
(Total sleep time / total time in bed) x 100
Assesses daytime somnolence and daytime **REM** onset in narcolepsy

blocks.caption: Shaded box titled "DREAMS" (page 11): dreaming occurs at all stages of sleep; non-REM dreams are thought-like, REM dreams may be illogical and bizarre.

blocks.text: Dreaming occurs at all stages of sleep but content varies: in non-**REM** sleep dreams are thought-like (as if solving a problem); in **REM** sleep they may be illogical and bizarre.

**REM** latency (sleep onset to first **REM**) is about 90 minutes in a polysomnogram, not 30, 60 or 160 minutes: a night has four or five cycles of 90-110 minutes, the first cycle ending with a brief arousal before **REM** at about 90 minutes; the first **REM** period lasts only 5-10 minutes whereas the last may last up to 40 minutes.

blocks.note: Notes define sleep latency but give no normal value. **Q40** explanation: normally about 15-20 minutes; more than 30 minutes can indicate insomnia.

bullets.text: Actigraphy = motion sensor for sleep-wake patterns; PSG = EEG + EMG + EOG (+ECG, oximetry, respiration).
PSG diagnoses sleep apnoea, narcolepsy, restless legs, REM behavioural disorder.
REM latency normally about 90 min in adults.
Sleep efficiency = total sleep time / time in bed x 100.
MSLT assesses daytime somnolence and sleep-onset REM in narcolepsy.
Non-REM dreams thought-like; REM dreams bizarre.

blocks.text: Average sleep length is about 7.5 hours per night, made up of **NREM** and **REM** phases.

blocks.caption: Four labelled boxes (page 11): Stage 1 NREM sleep (5%), Stage 2 NREM sleep (45%), Stage 3 NREM sleep (12%), Stage 4 NREM sleep (13%), each with the features printed in the box.

blocks.title: NREM stages
rows: Drowsy; when awoken, one denies being asleep; low-voltage theta activity, sharp V waves

blocks.text: ==75%== of adult sleep is **NREM**. Physiological functions are markedly lower than in wakefulness (decreased muscle tone, respiration, temperature and heart rate). Stages 3 and 4 together constitute slow wave sleep (**SWS**), which dominates the initial part of sleep.

**NREM** features: increased parasympathetic activity (decreased heart rate, systolic blood pressure, respiratory rate, cerebral blood flow); abolition of tendon reflexes; upward ocular deviation with few or no movements.
**NREM** gives reduced recall of dreams if awoken. Sleep terror is an **NREM** disorder: afterwards children appear confused and do not recall what terrified them.

==25%== of adult sleep is **REM**. Darting eye movements occur despite paralysis of other muscles; brain activity and physiological activity resemble wakefulness. **EEG**: low-voltage mixed-frequency (theta and slow alpha) activity, with sawtooth waves.
A typical night has five **NREM**/**REM** cycles; **REM** episodes lengthen as the night goes on.

**REM** features: increased sympathetic activity (increased heart rate, systolic blood pressure, respiratory rate, cerebral blood flow); active autonomic functions with penile erection or increased vaginal blood flow; increased protein synthesis; maximal loss of muscle tone with occasional myoclonic jerks; vivid dream recall (nightmares occur in **REM** and are well recollected).
In **REM** sleep behavioural disorder muscular paralysis does not occur, producing violent movements coinciding with brain activity.

blocks.title: NREM vs REM sleep
rows: Increased parasympathetic; **HR**, **BP**, respiration, cerebral blood flow decreased
Increased sympathetic; **HR**, **BP**, respiration, cerebral blood flow increased
Decreased muscle tone; abolition of tendon reflexes
Maximal loss of muscle tone (atonia), occasional myoclonic jerks

blocks.text: Increased recall of dreams on awakening is the **REM** feature; options such as abolition of tendon reflexes, increased parasympathetic activity, reduced heart rate and reduced cerebral blood flow are **NREM** features. In **REM**, autonomic activity increases (raised pulse, blood pressure, intracranial pressure, cerebral blood flow, erections) despite flaccid muscle paralysis.

The **INCORRECT** **REM** statement is muscle tone similar to awake state: **REM** has atonia (peripheral muscle paralysis), while **EEG** activity like wake, rapid eye movements, cardiac activity like wake and penile erection are all correct **REM** features.

bullets.text: REM = 25% of adult sleep; about 5 NREM/REM cycles per night, REM episodes lengthen.
NREM = 75% of adult sleep: Stage 1 5%, Stage 2 45%, Stage 3 12%, Stage 4 13%; SWS = stages 3 and 4.
Stage 2: spindles and K complexes; Stage 3 <50% delta; Stage 4 >50% delta.
NREM: parasympathetic, low HR/BP/RR/cerebral flow, tendon reflexes abolished, poor dream recall; sleep terror.
REM: sympathetic, high HR/BP/cerebral flow, erection, atonia with myoclonic jerks, vivid dreams, nightmares.
REM behavioural disorder: no paralysis, violent movements.

sections.title: 17. Physiology of sleep: brain activity patterns

blocks.title: Sleep-specific waveforms
rows: Upper alpha or lower beta frequency, seen in many stages but especially stage 2; initial rise in amplitude that decreases slowly; usually <1 second; symmetric; most obvious in parasagittal regions

Large-amplitude delta frequency waves, sometimes with a sharp apex; throughout the brain but more prominent bifrontally; may be mediated by thalamocortical circuitry; usually symmetric; occur each time the patient is partially aroused; runs of generalised rhythmic theta sometimes follow (arousal burst)

Sharp waves largest at the vertex bilaterally, usually symmetrical; multiple V waves especially in stage 2; often follow sleep disturbances such as brief sounds and, like K complexes, may occur in brief semiarousals

blocks.text: K complexes are the stage 2 sleep waveform - not stage 3, stage 4, stage 1 or **REM**: the large multicomponent K complex and the rhythmic spindle are the hallmarks of **NREM** stage 2.

bullets.text: Spindles: upper alpha/lower beta, mainly stage 2, <1 s, parasagittal.
K complexes: large delta waves, bifrontal, follow partial arousals; arousal burst = theta run after K complex.
V waves: vertex sharp waves, mainly stage 2, may follow brief sounds.
Spindles and K complexes are stage 2 hallmarks.

sections.title: 18. Physiology of sleep: regulation and ageing

blocks.text: The master clock of the brain is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (**SCN**) in the anterior hypothalamus, orchestrating circadian rhythms and synchronised by retinal signals.

The **SCN** is reset daily by light: melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells project via the retinohypothalamic tract to the **SCN**, giving light input independent of vision. Without solar guidance the 24-hour cycle lengthens to about 26 hours (free-running).
Pineal **melatonin** secreted in darkness can also reset the **SCN**, so **melatonin** promotes sleep in delayed sleep onset or jet lag.

The ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (**VLPO**) is the sleep switch nucleus; it induces sleep by inhibiting the arousal nuclei, and **VLPO** damage causes chronic insomnia. **VLPO** must be inhibited for waking, through negative feedback from the monoaminergic system; the switch to arousal is stabilised by orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the hypothalamus, active mainly in wakefulness. Narcolepsy involves reduced orexin neurons and repeated daytime somnolence.

blocks.caption: Table "Ascending Reticular Activating System - Neurotransmitters" (page 13): columns Neurotransmitter / Cell Bodies / Function; rows Cholinergic, Noradrenergic, Dopaminergic, Serotoninergic, Histaminergic.
Shaded box titled "SLEEP & AGEING" (page 13): newborn sleep, shift by 3-4 months, adult pattern by late teens, and changes in older persons.

blocks.title: Sleep and ageing
rows: About 16 hours a day; >==50%== in **REM**; sleep-onset **REM** seen
**REM** falls to less than ==40%== of sleep; sleep entered through initial **NREM**
Adult pattern established; relatively constant until old age
Absolute reduction in slow wave sleep and **REM**; more awakenings after sleep onset

blocks.text: The adult pattern of sleep (sleep entered through **NREM** rather than **REM**, as in infants) is established by 3 months, not 12 months, 18 months, 3 years or 5 years: newborn sleep onset is through **REM** and each episode is only one or two cycles (versus four or more in adults); by 3 months **melatonin** and cortisol rhythms are established with **NREM** at sleep onset.

blocks.note: Notes describe **REM** sleep behaviour disorder (no muscle paralysis) but not what it is associated with. Mock **Q66**: Lewy body disease is the answer - **RBD** is associated with Parkinson disease, multi-system atrophy and Guillain-Barre syndrome and may be the prodrome of neurodegenerative disorders such as dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson disease.

blocks.text: Cholinergic stimulation is the answer key for the receptor whose stimulation leads to sleep onset (noradrenergic, 5HT2, glucocorticoid and histaminergic receptors are the distractors): the explanation contrasts cholinergic **REM-ON** neurons in the tegmentum, which fire during **REM**, with noradrenergic **REM-OFF** neurons in the locus coeruleus, which stop firing in **REM** - the two fire reciprocally.
The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus is the monitor of the circadian rhythm - not hippocampus, locus ceruleus, nucleus accumbens or dorsal medial thalamus.

Dysfunctional orexin (hypocretin) neurons = narcolepsy (not obesity, catatonia, chorea or anorexia): narcolepsy with cataplexy shows profound loss of orexin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, and orexin stabilises wakefulness by stimulating release of wake-promoting neurotransmitters.

Excessive daytime somnolence with collapse on laughing (cataplexy) = narcolepsy, and low hypocretin (orexin) is the risk factor to pick: low **CSF** hypocretin-1 is highly specific (==99.1%==) and sensitive (==88.5%==) for narcolepsy with cataplexy.

bullets.text: SCN (anterior hypothalamus) = master clock, reset by light via melanopsin retinal ganglion cells and retinohypothalamic tract; free-running about 26 hours.
Melatonin can reset SCN; helps delayed sleep onset and jet lag.
VLPO = sleep switch; damage causes chronic insomnia; orexin neurons stabilise arousal; reduced in narcolepsy.
Cholinergic = REM-on; noradrenergic (locus coeruleus) = REM-off; 5HT2 and H1 maintain arousal.
Newborn 16 h/day with >50% REM; REM <40% by 3-4 months; adult pattern by late teens; elderly lose SWS and REM.
Cholinergic REM-ON neurons (tegmentum) vs noradrenergic REM-OFF neurons (locus coeruleus).

blocks.title: Effects on sleep architecture
rows: Increases **SWS** (chronic use: loss of **SWS**); reduces initial **REM** but increases second-half **REM**
Increased stage 1 sleep; reduced **REM** with normal **REM** latency; reduced slow wave sleep
Decrease sleep latency; increase sleep time; reduce stage 1; increase stage 2; reduce **REM** and **SWS**; **REM** rebound on cessation; prevent transition from stage 2 into deep stages 3 and 4
Increased sleep latency and fragmentation; reduced sleep time
Loss of **SWS** (first half); increased **REM** (leading to early awakening); reduced **REM** latency
Inconsistent reduction in **REM** latency and slow wave sleep; antipsychotics have variable effects
Alerting due to 5HT2 stimulation; may reduce **REM** latency; variable **REM** suppression
Reduce sleep time by decreasing both **REM** and **SWS**; **REM** rebound on cessation (except **modafinil**)
Less effect on sleep architecture; **zopiclone** may increase **SWS**

blocks.forTopic: REM-suppressing drugs in the sleep table
blocks.mnemonic: Big Cats Chase Lazy Old Sleepy Tigers

blocks.text: Benzodiazepines for insomnia **REDUCE** stage 1 sleep: the explanation lists decreased sleep latency, increased sleep time, reduced stage 1, increased stage 2, reduced **REM** and slow wave sleep, and **REM** rebound on cessation - so increased slow wave sleep, reduced stage 2, increased **REM** and reduced **REM** latency are wrong.

**REM** rebound on cessation is the stimulant (**methylphenidate**) answer; **modafinil** is the named exception and is a distractor in the same option list (**zolpidem**, SSRIs and inhalants are the others): stimulants reduce total sleep time by decreasing both **REM** and slow wave sleep.

items.text: Atonia is the characteristic **REM** feature (reduced recall of dreaming, decreased heart rate, abolition of tendon reflexes and upward ocular deviation are not).
Slow wave sleep = stages 3 and 4 of **NREM** (slow delta waves predominate); not stages 1 and 2 or 2 and 3.
**REM** sleep predominates in neonates (16-20 hours of sleep a day, about ==50%== of it **REM**).
Peak cortisol about 6 **AM** (asked again with options 10 **AM**, 4 **AM**, 8 **AM**, 6 **AM**, 2 **PM**).
The suprachiasmatic nucleus controls the biological clock of internal circadian rhythms (not attention, long-term memory, sexual behaviour or water and hunger).

bullets.text: Benzodiazepines: shorter latency, less stage 1, more stage 2, less REM and SWS, REM rebound on stopping.
Depression: reduced REM latency, increased REM, loss of first-half SWS.
Lithium and carbamazepine: suppress REM, raise REM latency, increase SWS.
Stimulants: reduce REM and SWS; REM rebound on cessation except modafinil.
Tricyclics suppress REM (esp. clomipramine); SSRIs alerting via 5HT2.
Alcohol withdrawal: intense REM rebound; loss of SWS.
Methylphenidate (stimulant) gives REM rebound on cessation; modafinil is the exception.

sections.title: 20. Neurophysiological measurements: EEG basics and waveforms

blocks.text: **EEG** records brain electrical activity. In psychiatric practice it is primarily used to rule out seizures, monitor **ECT** and in polysomnography for sleep disorders.

Standard **EEG** uses 21 scalp electrodes placed by the 10/20 International System: distances between landmarks on the head are measured and electrodes placed at 10 or 20 percent of that distance in an anterior-posterior or transverse direction.

blocks.title: Activation procedures
rows: Can activate paroxysmal discharges in some cases
Can be used when the wake tracing is normal

blocks.caption: Table "Wave forms noted in EEG" (page 15): Waves / Frequency / Notes for Beta, Alpha, Theta, Delta, Mu, Lambda.

blocks.title: EEG wave forms
rows: Some seen frontal/central in normal waking **EEG**
Dominant frequency with eyes closed and relaxed; occipitoparietal; disappears with anxiety, arousal, eye opening or focused attention; dominance reduces with age
Small sporadic amount in waking **EEG** at frontotemporal area; prominent in drowsy or sleep **EEG**; excessive theta awake is pathological
Not seen in waking **EEG**; common in deeper sleep; focal/generalised delta awake is pathological
Over the motor cortex; arch-like waves; attenuated by movement of the contralateral limb
Single occipital triangular symmetrical sharp wave from visual scanning when awake or in light sleep

blocks.text: Beta and alpha are fast waves; theta and delta are slow waves.

blocks.caption: Five-box row (page 15): Newborns, Infants, Early childhood, Mid-adolescence, Adults, each with the EEG description printed in its box.

blocks.title: EEG across development
rows: Irregular medium- to high-voltage delta activity
Alpha range develops in posterior areas

blocks.text: Ongoing delta activity when awake is almost always abnormal in an awake adult - that is the **TRUE** statement. Beta activity is **NOT** abnormal in adults (not uncommon over frontal-central regions), alpha is the dominant eyes-closed rhythm (not abolished by closing the eyes), and delta is absent from the normal waking **EEG**.

A normal awake **EEG** in a 3-month-old shows prominent delta and theta waves (irregular medium- to high-voltage delta, 3.5 Hz or less, gradually giving way to faster rhythmic activity); spindles, alpha/beta, mu/lambda and K complexes are the distractors.
Focusing attention on a cognitive task abolishes alpha waves (alpha block) - alpha does not appear on focusing attention and theta is not the rhythm that disappears.

Alpha is maximal over the occipital region (the correct statement). The wrong options: antipsychotics do not abolish alpha (neuroleptics commonly increase it), alpha does not reduce with eye closure, it is a lower frequency band than beta (8-13 Hz, oscillating about 10 times per second), and in Huntington disease alpha is poorly formed or absent rather than in excess.

Hyperventilation and photic stimulation (stroboscopic light) are the two most commonly used activation techniques and may provoke epileptiform discharges - even seizures - in primary or genetic generalised epilepsy; the answer key for the photic-stimulation spike-wave stem is generalised seizures (not absence seizures, myoclonic epilepsy, **CJD** or Angelman syndrome).

blocks.subtopic: EEG yield in epilepsy and activation
blocks.note: Notes do not give **EEG** yield in epilepsy. **Q1** explanation: outpatient **EEG** detects epileptiform abnormalities in only 29-==55%== of patients with focal epilepsy (answer 30-==50%== normal between attacks). **Q36** explanation: hyperventilation and photic stimulation are the two most commonly used activation techniques.

bullets.text: EEG uses: rule out seizures, monitor ECT, polysomnography; 21 electrodes, 10/20 system.
Activation: hyperventilation (most common), photic stimulation, sleep deprivation, sleep recording.
Beta >13 Hz; alpha 8-13 Hz; theta 4-8 Hz; delta <4 Hz.
Alpha: eyes closed, relaxed, occipitoparietal; abolished by arousal/eye opening.
Awake delta or excess theta = pathology.
Adult EEG appearance by 12-14 years.

blocks.caption: Table "EEG in various disorders" (page 16): Disorder / EEG finding, rows from Absence seizures (petit-mal) to Structural lesions.

blocks.title: EEG in various disorders
rows: Rarely normal in advanced dementia; may help differentiate pseudodementia from dementia

Changes notable by age 2; prolonged runs of high-amplitude 2-3 Hz frontal activity with superimposed interictal epileptiform discharges at all ages; occipital high-amplitude rhythmic 4-6 Hz activity facilitated by eye closure under age 12; no difference with or without seizures
Increased incidence of **EEG** abnormalities in those with aggressive behaviour
Positive spikes (14 and 6 per second) in ==25%== of patients
Generalised periodic 1-2 Hz sharp waves in nearly ==90%== of sporadic **CJD**; less often in familial/hormonal transplant-related forms; **NOT** seen in variant form
Focal slowing (sharply focal trauma); focal delta slowing (subdural haematomas)
Slowed alpha frequency and increased generalised theta slowing
Episodic discharges recurring every 1-3 seconds with variable focal waves over the temporal areas
Initial loss of alpha; later flattened trace

Hypsarrhythmia (diffuse high-voltage >400 microvolt giant waves with chaotic background of irregular asynchronous multifocal spikes and sharp waves); seizures associated with marked background suppression (electrodecremental response)
Diffuse, often synchronous, high-voltage slowing (acute encephalitis)
Diffuse generalised slowing; triphasic waves 1.5-3.0 per second high-voltage slow waves especially in hepatic encephalopathy
Non-specific diffuse increase in slow waves
Paroxysmal changes consistent with partial seizure activity in one-third; focal slowing in about ==25%==
Generalised, hemispheric or focal spike / spike-wave discharge

blocks.text: Diffuse slowing of background is the most common **EEG** abnormality; it is nonspecific and signifies encephalopathy. Focal slowing suggests local mass lesions (oedema, haematoma, focal seizure).
Interictal epileptiform discharges are a hallmark of seizure disorder but not a common finding; if lateralised and periodic they may suggest an acute destructive brain lesion.

A 1-2 Hz bi- or triphasic sharp- and slow-wave pattern is **CJD** (hepatic encephalopathy, Huntington, Alzheimer and multi-infarct dementia are the distractors); it may appear only very late or need repeated testing, and the earliest **EEG** finding is more often rhythmic generalised slowing. The notes add that this pattern is **NOT** seen in the variant form.

Triphasic waves (1.5-3.0 per second high-voltage slow waves) point to hepatic encephalopathy, but only about half of patients with triphasic waves have it - the rest have other toxic-metabolic encephalopathies, so the pattern is not specific to the liver.

Regular 3 Hz complexes = absence seizures (the characteristic three-per-second spike-and-wave of petit mal). The other options have different **EEG** findings in the notes: **ADHD** spike/spike-waves, **CJD** periodic 1-2 Hz sharp waves, Angelman 2-3 Hz frontal activity, antisocial personality disorder only an increased incidence of abnormalities.
A flattened **EEG** trace is Huntington disease (marked voltage reduction with absent alpha rhythm, sometimes flat traces) - not petit mal epilepsy, **CJD**, delirium or partial seizures.

In Alzheimer dementia the **EEG** usually shows generalised background slowing (slowing and shortened alpha rhythm); periodic frontal-lobe discharges and spike-and-wave are not the pattern - periodic sharp-wave/spike discharges belong to **CJD**, and **EEG** is otherwise not especially helpful in separating the common causes of dementia.

items.text: Theta = 4 to 8 Hz (alpha 8-13 Hz, beta faster than 13 Hz, delta 3.5 Hz or less).
Delta = less than 4 Hz (distractors 13-40 Hz, 8-13 Hz, 3.5-7.5 Hz, 7-11 Hz).
Alpha is the trace with eyes closed during relaxation (not gamma, beta, theta or delta).
Infants have a dominant rhythm of about 3 Hz (delta), not 10 Hz.
More than 13 Hz = beta (alpha 8-13, theta 4-8, delta less than 4).
Beta waves are the low-amplitude, high-frequency (more than 13 Hz) rhythm.
During relaxed wakefulness a normal **EEG** shows alpha (8-13 Hz) - not delta, gamma, beta or theta.
Angelman syndrome **EEG** changes are notable by age 2 (epilepsy onset most prevalent at 1-3 years).

blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q14**: high-amplitude repetitive bilaterally synchronous polyphasic sharp and slow wave complexes every 4-15 seconds indicate **SSPE** (periodic sharp-wave complexes or burst-suppression); distinguished from **CJD**, which also shows periodic discharges.

bullets.text: Absence: regular 3 Hz; CJD: generalised periodic 1-2 Hz (sporadic; not variant).
Hepatic/metabolic: triphasic waves 1.5-3 per second.
Huntington: loss of alpha then flat trace; infantile spasms: hypsarrhythmia.
Angelman: changes by age 2; frontal 2-3 Hz runs; occipital 4-6 Hz under 12.
Herpes simplex encephalitis: temporal discharges every 1-3 s.
Diffuse slowing is the commonest abnormality; focal slowing suggests mass lesion.

blocks.title: Psychotropics
rows: Slowing of beta activity with increase in alpha, theta and delta activity
Slowing of beta activity with increase in alpha, theta and delta activity
Slowing of alpha or paroxysmal activity

blocks.title: Primarily sedating drugs (decrease alpha)

Increased frontal alpha; overall slow alpha

blocks.text: Benzodiazepines are the class that increases beta activity: they (like barbiturates) produce excessive diffuse fast activity, which may be a telltale sign of surreptitious drug use; **lithium**, anticonvulsants, antipsychotics and antidepressants are not the beta-increasing options.
On **sulpiride** (an antipsychotic) expect **SLOWING** of beta activity with increased alpha, theta and delta - not decreased alpha, decreased delta/theta or new-onset spike-and-wave.

blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q10** explanation: after **ECT** series, post-synaptic beta-adrenergic receptors are downregulated (as with virtually all antidepressant treatments); effects on serotonergic neurons controversial.

bullets.text: Antipsychotics/antidepressants: slow beta, more alpha/theta/delta.
Anticonvulsants: no effect on awake EEG; lithium slows alpha or paroxysmal activity.
Benzodiazepines: more beta, less alpha; barbiturates: beta in intoxication, spikes in withdrawal.
Opioids: less alpha, more theta/delta.
Alcohol/marijuana/cocaine/nicotine raise alpha; alcohol withdrawal raises beta; DTs fast beta.
Benzodiazepines increase beta activity; antipsychotics slow beta with more alpha, theta, delta.

blocks.text: Magnetoencephalography (**MEG**) measures magnetic fields produced by brain electrical activity; magnetic fields are less distorted by the skull and scalp than electric fields.

Scalp **EEG** is sensitive to tangential and radial components of a current source; **MEG** detects only the tangential component, so it may selectively measure activity in the sulci, whereas **EEG** measures sulci and the tops of gyri.

An **ERP** is a stereotyped change in electrical brain activity time-locked to an event (e.g. a stimulus; it can also occur for omission of an expected stimulus). ERPs are small relative to background **EEG** (low signal-to-noise ratio), so **ERP** averaging is often used.

ERPs have polarity (P or N) and latency (moment of peak after the stimulus, often the number in the label). **EEG**, **MEG** and **ERP** have much higher temporal resolution than fMRI, **SPECT** and **PET** but lack the high spatial resolution of **MR** techniques.

blocks.caption: Three labelled boxes (page 18): Early ERPs, Midlatency ERPs, Late ERPs, each with the bullet points printed in the box.

blocks.title: ERP classes by time of occurrence
rows: Study basic sensory pathways; also called evoked potentials (EPs) or brain stem evoked responses (**BAER**); to sounds (**AEP**), flashes (**VEP**) or electrical stimulation (**SEP**)
Occur after **BAER**; **N100**, **P50** and **P200**; amplitudes reduce with repetition (habituation / sensory gating)
Study cognitive pathways (attention, emotion, memory tasks); **P300** and **MMN** are late ERPs

blocks.text: **P300** is a positive late **ERP** around 300 ms after stimulus, generated when a rare target is embedded among frequent stimuli (auditory oddball); it relates to maintenance of working memory. Reduced **P300** amplitude is a well-established biological trait marker in schizophrenia.

Mismatch negativity (**MMN**) is a negative **ERP** at 100-200 ms to low-probability deviant sounds in a standard sequence when the participant is not attending; best seen in the difference wave. It reflects involuntary auditory information processing - comparison with a memory trace; decreased **MMN** amplitude is noted in schizophrenia.

Contingent negative variation (**CNV**) is a slow negative shift between two paired stimuli (**S1** cue, **S2** imperative stimulus). **CNV** reduction at central midline electrodes is noted in schizophrenia, especially with long illness duration and positive symptoms.

blocks.title: ERP findings in schizophrenia
rows: Reduced at central midline electrodes, esp. long illness with positive symptoms

blocks.note: Notes describe **P50** as a midlatency **ERP** that habituates (sensory gating) but not which structure regulates it. Mock **Q68**: **P50** suppression, a proposed endophenotype in schizophrenia, is regulated by wide-ranging neural circuitry prominently involving the hippocampus.

Not in the notes. **Q16**: rTMS for depression uses coil placement over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. **Q34** explanation: rTMS or tDCS may modulate abnormal sensorimotor networks in dystonia.

blocks.text: rTMS for depression is applied over the **LEFT** prefrontal region - specifically the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex - not right temporal, occipital or parietal, nor left temporal; applying rTMS at left **DLPFC** can enhance its connectivity with regions crucial for regulating emotional processing.

blocks.note: Not in the notes. **Q34**: rTMS is the innovative treatment with some beneficial effect in dystonia (other options: vagal nerve stimulation, leucotomy, behavioural reversal therapy, nerve ablation); the explanation says rTMS or tDCS may modulate abnormal sensorimotor networks and restore motor control.

Not in the notes. Mock **Q69** (depression after self-harm, social isolation, somatic back pain, constipation, isolated high serum calcium): hyperparathyroidism is the answer - primary hyperparathyroidism is generally related to parathyroid adenomas; most patients are asymptomatic but can have recurrent kidney stones, peptic ulcers, dehydration, constipation and altered mental status; confirm with parathyroid hormone levels.

bullets.text: MEG: magnetic fields less distorted by skull; detects tangential sources only (sulci).
ERP: time-locked, small, needs averaging; polarity and latency.
EEG/MEG/ERP have high temporal but low spatial resolution vs fMRI/PET/SPECT.
Early (BAER/EPs), midlatency (N100, P50, P200; sensory gating), late (P300, MMN) ERPs.
P300 (about 300 ms, oddball, working memory) reduced in schizophrenia.
MMN (100-200 ms, deviant sounds) decreased in schizophrenia; CNV reduced at central midline.
